title: God watched over the first men
source_text: Καὶ ὁ θεῖος δὲ κατὰ Μωϋσέα λόγος εἰσήγαγε τοὺς πρώτους ἀκούοντας θειοτέρας φωνῆς καὶ χρησμῶν καὶ ὁρῶντας ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε ἀγγέλων θεοῦ ἐπιδημίας γεγενημένας πρὸς αὐτούς. καὶ γὰρ εἰκὸς ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ κόσμου ἐπὶ πλεῖον βεβοηθῆσθαι τὴν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν· ἕως προκοπῆς γενομένης εἰς σύνεσιν καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς ἀρετὰς καὶ τὴν εὕρεσιν τῶν τεχνῶν δυνηθῶσι καὶ καθ᾿ ἑαυτοὺς ζῆν, οὐ χρῄζοντες ἀεὶ ἐπιτροπευόντων καὶ οἰκονομούντων αὐτοὺς μετὰ παραδόξου ἐπιφανείας τῶν ὑπηρετουμένων τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ βουλήματι. ἀκόλουθον δὲ τούτοις τὸ ψεῦδος εἶναι ὅτι κατ᾿ ἀρχὰς ἄνθρωποι μὲν ὑπὸ θηρίων ἡρπάζοντο καὶ ἠσθίοντο, θηρία δ᾿ ὑπ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἥκιστα ἡλίσκετο. ἐκ δὴ τούτων φανερὸν ὅτι ψεῦδος καὶ τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου οὕτως λεγόμενον· ὥστε ταύτῃ γε ὁ θεὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους μᾶλλον τοῖς θηρίοις ὑπέβαλεν. οὐ γὰρ ὑπέβαλε τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τοῖς θηρίοις ὁ θεὸς, ἀλλὰ τῇ συνέσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἁλωτὰ δέδωκεν εἶναι τὰ θηρία καὶ ταῖς ἀπὸ συνέσεως ὑφισταμέναις κατ᾿ ἐκείνων τέχναις. οὐ γὰρ ἀθεεὶ ἐμηχανήσαντο σφίσιν αὐτοῖς οἱ ἄνθρωποι σωτηρίαν ἀπὸ τῶν θηρίων καὶ τὴν κατ᾿ ἐκείνων ἐπικράτειαν.
pass_a_gloss: And the divine word (θεῖος λόγος) according to Moses (κατὰ Μωϋσέα) introduced (εἰσάγω) the first ones hearing (ἀκούω) a more divine voice (θειοτέρα φωνή) and oracles (χρησμός) and seeing sometimes (ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε) sojourns/visits (ἐπιδημία) of angels of God (ἄγγελοι θεοῦ) having come to them. For it is likely (εἰκός) that in the beginning of the world the nature of men was helped (βοηθέω) more, until, progress (προκοπή) having come about toward understanding (σύνεσις) and the remaining virtues (ἀρετή) and the finding (εὕρεσις) of the arts, they could live also by themselves (καθ᾿ ἑαυτούς), not always needing (χρῄζω) those acting as guardians (ἐπιτροπεύω) and managing (οἰκονομέω) them with marvellous appearance (παράδοξος ἐπιφάνεια), of those serving (ὑπηρετέω) the will (βούλημα) of God. Consequent (ἀκόλουθον) on these is that it is a falsehood (ψεῦδος) that at the beginnings men were snatched and eaten by beasts, but beasts least of all were caught by men. From these it is clear (φανερός) that false also is what is said thus by Celsus: 'so that in this way at least God rather subjected (ὑποβάλλω) men to the beasts.' For God did not subject men to the beasts, but gave the beasts to be catchable (ἁλωτός) by the understanding of men and by the arts against them that subsist (ὑφίσταμαι) from understanding. For not without God (οὐκ ἀθεεί) did men contrive (μηχανάομαι) for themselves safety (σωτηρία) from the beasts and mastery (ἐπικράτεια) over them.
pass_b_english: The divine account in Moses, too, shows the first men hearing a more divine voice and oracles (Genesis 3:8), and sometimes seeing visits made to them by angels of God (Genesis 18:1–2; 19:1). For it is likely that at the beginning of the world human nature was given more help, until, having made progress in understanding and the other virtues and in the discovery of the arts, men could live on their own as well, without always needing those who serve the will of God to guard and manage them through wondrous appearances.

It follows from this that it is false to say that at the beginning men were carried off and eaten by wild beasts, while wild beasts were very seldom caught by men. From this, then, it is clear that what Celsus says in these words is also false: “So in this respect, at least, it was rather men that God made subject to the beasts.” For God did not make men subject to the beasts. Rather, he granted that the beasts should be caught by human understanding and by the arts against them that arise from understanding. For it was not without God that men contrived for themselves safety from the beasts and mastery over them.

choices.choice: 'divine word in Moses' -> 'divine account in Moses' so lowercase logos is not confused with the Word
Celsus's 'mallon' made explicit: 'it was rather men that God made subject to the beasts'
Restored the contrast of 'alla': 'Rather, he granted'
Kept Genesis 3:8 and 18:1-2/19:1 as representative citations for the general reference; noted as such

Origen refers generally to the Mosaic narratives of the first ages rather than quoting a verse. The inline citations mark the clearest instances: the first men hearing the voice of the Lord God (Genesis 3:8; compare 2:16–17) and angels visiting Abraham and Lot (Genesis 18:1–2; 19:1); other angelic visits (for example Genesis 16:7) also fit. The citations are representative, not Origen's own. Celsus's sentence 'So in this respect...' is quoted directly in the Greek. οὐκ ἀθεεί ('not without God') is a Homeric phrase (compare Odyssey 18.353) but used here as ordinary idiom; not cited. The thought that God gave the beasts to human mastery may echo Genesis 1:28, but there is no verbal quotation; not cited inline.
